comment: Site Audit guidance corpus. Original paraphrased summaries with source links - never copied text. checkIds map chunks to finding ids deterministically; embeddings are added by scripts/embed-knowledge.mjs (runs on the dev machine, never on the server) into knowledge.embedded.json.

chunks.title: Title tags that survive the results page
chunks.content: Google rewrites titles it considers weak, and truncates around 580 pixels - roughly 55 to 60 characters. A good title leads with the page's distinct topic, reads as a promise the page keeps, and avoids repeating the site name on every page. One title per page, unique across the site.

chunks.title: Meta descriptions set the snippet, not the ranking
chunks.content: Descriptions do not affect ranking directly, but they are the ad copy of the result: when missing or weak, search engines assemble a snippet from page text, often badly. Keep them under roughly 155 characters, specific to the page, and front-load the value. Every page gets its own.

chunks.title: Canonical links consolidate duplicate signals
chunks.content: When the same content answers on several URLs (tracking parameters, http vs https, trailing slashes), ranking signals split between them. A rel=canonical on every page - usually pointing at itself - tells crawlers which URL is the one to index and credit. It is a hint, not a directive, but a strong one.

chunks.title: Open Graph controls how shares render
chunks.content: og:title, og:description and og:image decide what a shared link looks like in chats and feeds; twitter:card selects the large-image layout on X. Without them platforms guess, often rendering a bare URL nobody clicks. The image should be 1200x630 and hosted on a stable URL.

chunks.title: JSON-LD is how machines read your page
chunks.content: Structured data in JSON-LD is the format Google recommends for rich results and the format AI systems parse most reliably. A broken block is worse than none - it fails silently and takes eligible rich results with it. Validate after every change, match the @type to the real content, and never mark up content that is not visible on the page.
chunks.sourceName: Google Search Central - Structured data guidelines

chunks.title: Choosing the right schema.org type
chunks.content: schema.org defines the vocabulary: WebPage is the safe default, Article for editorial content, Product for things with offers, FAQPage for genuine question lists, HowTo for stepped instructions, Organization and WebSite once on the home page. Richer, accurate types earn richer results; wrong types earn manual actions.

chunks.title: Headings are the machine-readable outline
chunks.content: One h1 stating the page topic, then h2/h3 in order without skipping levels. Crawlers, screen readers and AI summarizers all reconstruct the document from this outline; jumps and duplicate h1s blur what the page is about. Headings should describe sections, not decorate them.
chunks.sourceName: Google Search Central - SEO Starter Guide

chunks.title: Alt text serves three consumers at once
chunks.content: Alt text is how screen readers speak an image, how image search indexes it, and how AI systems understand it. Describe what the image shows in the page's context; leave alt empty (alt="") only for purely decorative images so assistive tech skips them.
chunks.sourceName: Google Search Central - Images best practices

chunks.title: The viewport meta is the mobile baseline
chunks.content: Google indexes the mobile version of pages first. Without a viewport meta the page renders desktop-wide on phones, fails mobile-friendliness, and loses ranking on mobile queries - which are most queries. width=device-width with initial-scale=1 is the standard declaration.
chunks.sourceName: Google Search Central - Mobile site best practices

chunks.title: Declare the page language
chunks.content: The lang attribute on the html element tells screen readers which voice to use and helps search engines serve the page to the right language audience. Set it to the primary language of the visible content, for example lang="en" or lang="hi".

chunks.title: robots.txt is the crawler contract
chunks.content: robots.txt tells crawlers what they may fetch. A missing file means everything is fair game, which is usually fine - but an explicit file lets you protect admin paths, point at the sitemap, and set per-bot policy. It controls crawling, not indexing: blocked pages can still appear in results from external links.

chunks.title: AI crawlers decide whether AI answers can cite you
chunks.content: GPTBot (OpenAI), ClaudeBot (Anthropic), PerplexityBot, Google-Extended (Gemini training) and CCBot (Common Crawl) each honor robots.txt. Blocking them keeps your content out of AI training and answers - a legitimate choice - but sites that want to be cited by AI assistants must allow the bots that feed those answers. The trade is traffic-from-citation versus content control; decide it deliberately per bot.

chunks.title: Sitemaps make discovery independent of links
chunks.content: A sitemap.xml lists the URLs you want crawled with optional lastmod dates. It matters most for new sites with few inbound links and large sites with deep pages. Keep lastmod honest - search engines learn to ignore sitemaps whose dates change on every deploy without content changes.

chunks.title: Content that only exists after JavaScript is invisible to most machines
chunks.content: Google renders JavaScript, but in a delayed second wave; most other crawlers and nearly all AI-answer fetchers read only the raw HTML. If the main content arrives via client-side rendering, those systems see an empty page. Server-side render or statically generate the content that must be found and cited.
chunks.sourceName: Google Search Central - JavaScript SEO basics

chunks.title: What makes content citeable by AI systems
chunks.content: AI assistants prefer to cite pages that state facts plainly: visible dates, named authors, direct answers near the top, and self-contained sections a model can quote without losing meaning. Undated pages read as unverifiable; answer-shaped headings and short factual paragraphs are quoted most.

chunks.title: HTTPS is the floor, not a bonus
chunks.content: HTTPS has been a ranking signal for years and browsers mark plain-http pages as not secure, which drives users away before content loads. Serve everything over https and 301 the http origin to it.
chunks.sourceName: Google Search Central - HTTPS as a ranking signal

chunks.title: Non-200 pages waste crawl and rank nothing
chunks.content: Pages that answer 404, 500 or redirect chains spend crawl budget and accumulate no ranking. Fix the link that led there, restore the content, or 301 to the closest living page. Soft-404s - a 200 page that says not found - are treated as errors too.
chunks.sourceName: Google Search Central - HTTP status codes

chunks.title: noindex removes pages deliberately
chunks.content: A noindex robots meta keeps a page out of search while still letting users and crawlers reach it. Right for thin utility pages, wrong when left on a page you want found - audit noindex flags to confirm each one is intentional.
chunks.sourceName: Google Search Central - Block search indexing
